To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the trunk is displaced forwards at the beginning of horizontal jumps, the activity of the bi-articular muscles is adapted to jump direction, and the mono-articular muscles are adapted to jump direction by timing of their activation rather than by peak amplitude.
the trunk is oriented more forward at the beginning, and knee extension moment is smaller in horizontal jumps than in vertical jumps.
maximal-effort horizontal and vertical jumps are characterized by differences in trunk and leg motion, knee extensor moment, and EMG activity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the human musculoskeletal system is controlled during the performance of complex movements.
the control of the body's centre of gravity during locomotion, in particular the role of the lower limbs in the control of the trunk.
the biomechanical and neuromuscular control mechanisms that are used to perform the complex motor task of a maximal effort standing jump.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the control of jump directions is achieved by a combination of (i) a forward displacement of the trunk at the beginning of push-off and (ii) an increase in the relative activation levels in the biarticular hamstrings during the push-off phase.

the primary difference between the HJ and VJ is the relative timing of activity in the biarticular muscles, rectus femoris, and hamstrings, which is responsible for the differences in knee joint torques.
the primary difference between the two jumps is the knee extension moment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the direction of a jump is controlled by the orientation of the trunk at the beginning of push off, the activation levels of the mono-articulate knee extensors, and the activation of the bi-articular rectus femories and hamstrings.

the trunk position and the activation patterns of the biartical rectus femoris, hamstrings, and knee extensors are adapted to control the knee and hip joint torques to meet the demands of the jump direction.

the trunk position at the beginning of push-off and the activation patterns of the biartricular rectus femoris, hamstrings, and mono-articular knee muscles are the main determinants for the control of direction of maximal effort standing jumps.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the direction of a jump can be controlled by adjusting the initial orientation of the trunk and the relative activity levels of the bi-articular rectus femorius and hamstring muscles.
there is an optimal trunk orientation for a given jump direction, and that trunk orientation at the initiation of the push-off can be used to control jump direction.

the control of jump directions in standing horizontal and jump is not only a result of differences in joint kinematics and kinetics between the two jumps but also a result of differences between the two jumps in the relative timing of activation of the biartricular rectus femoris, hamstrings, and monoarticular knee extensors.
